context: The input is choices = [1, 1, 2] at indices 0, 1, and 2. “First 1” and “second 1” distinguish indices 0 and 1. The figure marks the second 1 with a hat to identify it. Both have numerical value 1.
description: Black scissors prune indices already used on the current path. Backtracking makes those indices available again. Red scissors prune repeated values within one round. Each call creates its own duplicated set. It records only values actually chosen in that call after the black-scissors check, so its scope differs from that of selected.

Each square node represents a choice. Reading the choices from the root to a node gives the prefix shown in the table. A complete root-to-leaf path forms a permutation. The first table has separate columns for black and red scissors. Multiple candidates in a cell indicate multiple pruned branches. Red scissors prune the second 1 at root [] and at prefix [2]. Black scissors prune the other branches that reuse indices. The second table lists the three distinct permutations by number.

frames.explanation: A path can choose both 1s in succession because they have distinct indices. Within any one round, only one branch is expanded for the value 1.
frames.title: Two permutation pruning rules: indices and values

summary: Compare pruning repeated indices on a path (selected) with pruning repeated values in a round (duplicated).

tables.caption: One round of choices for each prefix
headers: Black scissors: skip an index already in use
Red scissors: skip a value already tried this round
rows: Second 1: value 1 already tried this round
First 1: index 0 is already on the path
First 1 and second 1: both indices are in use
First 1 and 2: both indices are in use
2: index 2 is already on the path
Second 1: value 1 already tried this round
2 and first 1: both indices are in use
